info.bio:
Antoine "Fats" Domino nació en Nueva Orleans en 1928. Consumado pianista, toda su música está empapada de una alegría vital el sello propio de su ciudad natal.

Muchos creen que el primer rock and roll de la historia fué su sencillo de 1949 "The fat man",desde ese momento hasta finales de los 50, sus canciones llegaban fácilmente a los primeros puestos de las listas de "race records" (así se catalogaba a la música negra en aquellos años).

scenes.name: Rock'n'roll
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fusión de rhythm'n'blues y country, con mucho más peso del primero. Chuck Berry inventa en 1955 el rock'n'roll tal como se conocerá durante cincuenta años (la guitarra como instrumento protagonista, canciones propias que hablan a los adolescentes); Bo Diddley aporta el ritmo «hambone», Little Richard y Esquerita el histerismo y el maquillaje (el primer «decadence-rock»), Jerry Lee Lewis el piano feroz y Sun Records el rockabilly. Elvis Presley es, para Scaruffi, «la primera gran estafa del rock'n'roll». Buddy Holly y Eddie Cochran abren otra vía; en paralelo nacen el soul (Ray Charles), la exótica (Martin Denny, Esquivel), la música electrónica de cinta y, en Gran Bretaña, el skiffle.

mentions.author: Piero Scaruffi
mentions.text: …serious pretenders to the title of first rock'n'roll song (not just a title referencing the act of "rocking") begins with The Fat Man (1949), cut by Fats Domino, a New Orleans performer, which certainly sounded like a new kind of boogie. The man who is commonly credited with inventing the term "rock'n'roll"…

mentions.author: Piero Scaruffi
mentions.text: …？ The magazine "Billboard" introduces charts for "folk" and "race" records ？ Moondog virtually invents every future genre of rock music 1949 ？ Fats Domino cuts The Fat Man, a new kind of boogie ？ Hank Williams' Lovesick Blues reaches the top of the country charts 309

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Early Recognition (1949) - Piano Over Vocals
podcast.body: By 1949, Antoine Domino had achieved minor celebrity status within New Orleans' black music scene, primarily lauded for his exceptional piano skills rather than his singing. "By 1949, Dubinot had become a minor celebrity among black music fans in New Orleans, more for his piano playing than for his singing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Dominant Black Rock & Roll Star (1956)
podcast.body: By late 1956, after many white rockabilly acts had faded from the US charts, Fats Domino, alongside Little Richard and Chuck Berry, stood as one of the few black R&B stars consistently delivering rock and roll hits. At this time, the default image for a rock and roll star was a black man with a piano, and Domino was by far the biggest record seller in this category. "But in late 1956 that default image was a black man with a piano and the black man with a piano who was selling the most records by far was Fat Stomano."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Racial Context of 1956
podcast.body: Fats Domino's remarkable commercial success in 1956 occurred against a backdrop of intense racial tension and the burgeoning Civil Rights Movement. Events like the murder of Emmett Till, Rosa Parks' defiance, and escalating white supremacist violence highlighted the societal conflict, making rock and roll's appeal to white teenagers listening to black musicians a revolutionary force. "This, as much as anything musical, is the context you need to understand why rock and roll was seen as so revolutionary in 1956 in particular."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: "The Fat Man" Song Title Origin - Radio Show Influence
podcast.body: In 1949, Dave Bartholomew, inspired by "The Fat Man" radio show about a 237-pound detective, decided to capitalize on the popular title and associate it with Fats Domino, leading to the lyrical change from the drug-themed "Juncker's Blues" to "they call me The Fat Man because I weigh 200 pounds." "Dave Bartholomew heard the show, and realized that he could capitalize on the part of the film. He could capitalize on the popular title, and tie it into his fat singer, so instead of, they call me a Juncker because I'm loaded all the time, Domino sang, they call me The Fat Man because I weigh 200 pounds."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Albums for R&B Artists - Rarity in the 1950s
podcast.body: In the 1950s, it was highly unusual for R&B and blues artists to release albums, as their records were primarily sold to jukebox manufacturers rather than directly to consumers purchasing LPs. Imperial Records' decision to issue Fats Domino's first album after six years of singles indicated a significant shift in his audience towards white buyers with disposable income. "With him and Blues artists hardly ever put out albums in the fifties."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Antoine Domino's Dedication to Music - Manual Record Playback
podcast.body: As a youth, Antoine Domino demonstrated his profound love for music by manually turning records with his finger on a broken wind-up player to continue listening, highlighting his early dedication. "he would sit at the record player and manually turn the records using his finger so he could still listen to them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Audience Shift to White Consumers
podcast.body: The introduction of Fats Domino's first album marked a pivotal change in his audience, signifying that he was increasingly selling records to white individuals who had the financial means to purchase LPs. This contrasted sharply with his traditional black audience, who largely continued to buy 78s due to economic constraints. "He was selling to white people with money."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Blues Club Patronage
podcast.body: As a child, Jerry Lee Lewis would regularly sneak into a local blues club with an entirely Black clientele to watch performers like Fats Domino, Charles Brown, BB King, and Big Joe Turner until he was kicked out by the owner in the segregated South. "he would regularly sneak into a local blues club with an otherwise entirely black-cli-on-tail and hide under the table to watch people like Fat Stummino, Charles Brown, BB King, and Big Joe Turner."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Collaboration with Earl Palmer
podcast.body: Earl Palmer, a prominent session drummer, had previously played with Fats Domino (among others) at Cosimo Matassa's studio in New Orleans before moving to Los Angeles. "Earl Palmer...after his years of playing with Little Richard, Lloyd Price, and Fats Domino in Casamon-Mutasa's studio"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty: "You Send Me" by Sam Cooke

podcast.title: Concert Riots and Racial Blame
podcast.body: Throughout 1956, Fats Domino's concerts were frequently marred by riots, which contemporary news reports often attributed to his "pulsating jungle rhythms"—a overtly racist explanation. Despite Domino's efforts to cross over to country and older pop audiences with mellowed standards, the violence persisted, driven by racial prejudices against integrated audiences and music. "The riots which broke out at his shows throughout that year were blamed in contemporary news reports on his pulsating jungle rhythms and there's not even an attempt made to hide the racism in statements like that."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Considered for "The Girl Can't Help It" Theme
podcast.body: Fats Domino was a prominent artist considered for recording the theme tune to "The Girl Can't Help It," but Little Richard was ultimately chosen over him for the opportunity. "he had become big enough that he was chosen over Fats Domino to record the theme tune to the Girl Can't Help It"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 54: Keep A Knockin

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
podcast.body: Fats Domino was an early pioneer in rock and roll, identified as one of the "piano heroes" whose instrument was fundamental to the genre's formation. His contributions helped integrate elements of jazz, boogie-woogie, and barrel house into the emerging rock sound. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Piano Heroes

podcast.title: Early Sound System Favorite
podcast.body: Fats Domino was repeatedly named as a favorite artist played in the histories of the early Jamaican sound systems, alongside Louis Jordan and Wynonie Harris. He contributed to the New Orleans R&B style favored by sound system audiences. "The other artists who get repeatedly named in the histories of the early sound systems, along with Jordan and Harris, have fat stomino, Lloyd Price, Professor Longher."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 114: "My Boy Lollipop" by Millie

podcast.title: Fats Domino - Claim to First Rock Star
podcast.body: Fats Domino is presented as a strong candidate for the title of the "first rock star," given his early success and consistent style, which mirrored "The Fat Man." "if anyone can claim to be the first rock star, it's Fat Stomano, and as the music he was making was all in the same style as The Fat Man."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino and Dave Bartholomew - Consistent 1950s Sound
podcast.body: Fats Domino, often collaborating with Dave Bartholomew, maintained a consistent musical style throughout the 1950s, producing records that defined their signature sound. "Fat Stomano, usually with Dave Bartholomew, carried on making records that sounded just like this throughout the 50s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Braggadocio - Friendly Tone
podcast.body: Even when employing sexual bragging in songs like "The Fat Man," Fats Domino's friendly vocal delivery made him sound less aggressive than his contemporaries, giving the impression he didn't entirely mean the boasts. "Domino comes across as friendly, even when, as in a song like this, he's bragging sexually, he doesn't actually sound like he means it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Commercial Dominance - Second Only to Elvis
podcast.body: Fats Domino's sales in the 1950s surpassed every other rock and roll artist except Elvis, and he achieved an impressive streak of 39 consecutive charting hit singles extending into the early 1960s. "He outsold every other rock and roll artist of the 50s other than Elvis, and had 39 charting hit singles in a row in the 50s and early 60s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Dismissal by Roy Brown - Upstaging Incident
podcast.body: Fats Domino and his band were dismissed by Roy Brown after Domino sang several numbers on stage, with Brown asserting he was only paid to play piano, not to upstage the headliner. "Domino and his entire band got dropped by Brown after Domino sang a few numbers on stage himself during a show."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Early Struggles (Age 21)
podcast.body: At 21, despite local celebrity as a pianist, Fats Domino faced financial hardship, supporting a family while living in his in-laws' home, working a mattress factory job, and selling flavored syrups to make ends meet. "at age 21, Fat's Domino already had a family and was living in a room in his in-laws house with his wife and kids, working a day job at a mattress factory, and working a second job selling fresh dyes with syrups to kids to try to make ends meet."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Later Records - Saxophone Solos
podcast.body: Subsequent Fats Domino recordings frequently featured saxophone solos that emulated the trumpet-like vocalizations heard on "The Fat Man." "On later records, there'd be a saxophone solo doing much the same kind of thing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Live Repertoire - "Juncker's Blues"
podcast.body: "Juncker's Blues" was a staple in Fats Domino's live performances, known for consistently energizing audiences. "Domino had a few tunes that would always get the audience as going, and one of them was Juncker's Blues."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Performance Style - Dance-Oriented
podcast.body: In 1949, Fats Domino's performing style, characterized by its ability to make people happy and encourage dancing, was his most significant attribute, despite not fitting the image of a sex symbol. "he had a way of performing that made people happy and made them want to dance, and in 1949, that was the most important thing for a musician to do."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Persona - "Big Cheerful Fat Man"
podcast.body: Fats Domino presented a cheerful, substantial figure, a stark contrast to the emerging "mean and moody and slim" rock star archetype, and spoke Louisiana Creole as his primary language. "He was a big cheerful Fatman, who spoke Louisiana Creole as his first language."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Personal Life - Stability and Community Ties
podcast.body: Fats Domino maintained a stable personal life, remaining married to the same woman for 61 years, and despite his wealth, he continued to live in his lifelong neighborhood until Hurricane Katrina forced him to evacuate in 2005. "He remained married to the same woman for 61 years, and while he got himself a nice big house when he became rich, it was still in the same neighbourhood he'd lived in all his life, and he stayed there until Hurricane Katrina drove him out in 2005."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Piano Style - Triplet-Based Boogie Woogie
podcast.body: Fats Domino was renowned as one of the premier Boogie Woogie pianists, distinguished by a unique style heavily reliant on triplets, setting him apart from other pianists who often favored more direct rhythms. "He was known as one of the best Boogie Boogie players around, with a unique style based on triplets, rather than the more straightforward rhythms many Boogie pianists used."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Records - Massive Rock and Roll Sales
podcast.body: Fats Domino's records were universally recognized as rock and roll and achieved immense commercial success, selling in massive numbers. "Everyone called them rock and roll, and they sold in massive numbers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Reputation - "Nicest Man in Music"
podcast.body: Fats Domino earned a reputation as one of the nicest individuals in the music industry, a fact that ironically makes biographical information about him scarce compared to more controversial contemporaries. "Domino was known as one of the nicest men in the music industry, to the extent that it's difficult to find much biographic information about him, compared to any of his contemporaries."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Signature - Tenor Saxophone Solo
podcast.body: A tenor saxophone solo, typically placed two-thirds into the track, became a hallmark of Fats Domino's later recordings, with his own voice fulfilling this role on "The Fat Man." "Domino's later records almost all featured a tenisex solo, roughly two thirds of the way through the record. In this case, it's Domino's own voice doing the job."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Total Sales - Historical Significance
podcast.body: With estimated sales between 65 million and 110 million, Fats Domino was, as late as the early 1980s, considered among the highest-selling artists in the rock era, surpassed only by Elvis, The Beatles, and Michael Jackson. "Estimates of his sales vary between 65 million and 110 million, but as late as the early 80s, he was being seriously claimed that the only people who sold more records than him in the rock era were Elvis, The Beatles, and Michael Jackson."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Vocal Delivery - Reflecting Personality
podcast.body: Fats Domino's shy, friendly, humble, gracious, and cheerful personality was directly conveyed in his vocals, distinguishing him from the more aggressive rhythm and blues vocalists of his era. "He was shy, friendly, humble, gracious, and cheerful, and that all comes across in his vocals, while other rhythm and blues vocalists of the era were aggressive."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Vocal Style - Mills Brothers Influence and Trumpet Imitation
podcast.body: Fats Domino's vocal delivery on "The Fat Man" is likened to The Mills Brothers, and notably includes a trumpet imitation, a subtle yet present detail. "Domino's scattered vocals here are very reminiscent of the mill's brothers. There's a similarity in his trumpet imitation, which I've not seen any one pick up on, but is very real."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Vocals - Obvious Cheeriness
podcast.body: A key characteristic of Fats Domino's vocal performance was his undeniable cheerfulness, a quality that permeated his delivery. "what really matters with the vocal part is Domino's obvious cheeriness."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Fats Domino/Bartholomew Sound - Layered Rhythmic Complexity
podcast.body: The signature Domino/Bartholomew sound featured a complex layering: Earl Palmer's simple backbeat on drums, a bass line with a Treheo rhythm, an overlaid horn riff, and Fats Domino's piano playing fast triplets, creating intricate polyrhythms. "You'd have Earl Palmer and drums playing a simple backbeat, and then over that you'd lay the bass playing a traheo rhythm, and then over that you'd lay a horn riff, going across both those other rhythms, and over that you'd lay Domino's piano playing fast triplets."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Hurricane Katrina Tribute Album
podcast.body: After Hurricane Katrina destroyed his New Orleans home, Fats Domino became the recipient of widespread support from the music community, with acclaimed artists including Elton John, Dr. John, Paul McCartney, and Robert Plant uniting to record a tribute album specifically to raise funds for its rebuilding. "When your home is destroyed in a hurricane, everyone from Elton John to Dr. John, from Paul McCartney to Robert Plant, will come together to record a tribute album to help raise funds to rebuild it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Influence on Recording Sessions
podcast.body: Little Richard's first recording session for Specialty Records was held at Cosimo Matassa's Studio, where Fats Domino recorded, and utilized the same session musicians that Domino regularly employed. This was done because Specialty knew Richard liked Domino's music. "Blackwell and Roup made an agreement with Don Roby to buy out his contract for $600."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 34: "Tutti Frutti" by Little Richard

podcast.title: Jamaican Taste Preference (1960s)
podcast.body: In the early 1960s, Jamaican audiences continued to favor the music of artists like Fats Domino, even as American musical tastes began to change towards rock and roll. "Jamaican audiences wanted Louis Jordan, Fat Storner and Jean and Eunice, but the Americans wanted Elvis and Gerrilly Lewis and Bobby Daring."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 114: "My Boy Lollipop" by Millie

podcast.title: Longevity and Career Span
podcast.body: Fats Domino's career was exceptionally long-lasting, spanning from 1949 until his death in 2017 at the age of 89, encompassing multiple profound revolutions in popular music. His top 30 R&B chart hits alone extended from 1949 through 1964, demonstrating his remarkable ability to remain relevant and successful across changing musical eras, outlasting many of his contemporaries. "His top 30 Arv and B chart hit, spanned from 1949 through to 1964, a career that covers multiple revolutions in music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Medal of Arts Recipient
podcast.body: Fats Domino was honored with the Medal of Arts by two different U.S. Presidents. He initially received the medal from Bill Clinton, and later a replacement from George W. Bush after his first medal was lost during the devastation of Hurricane Katrina. "You get the Medal of Arts awarded to you by two presidents."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Pre-Rock Star Success
podcast.body: Fats Domino distinguished himself as the singular star from the pre-rock and roll era of R&B who not only endured but thrived and achieved greater prominence within the emerging rock and roll landscape. He was, alongside Elvis Presley, the most successful artist among the first wave of rock and roll pioneers. "He was the one star from the pre-rock days of Arunbe to last and thrive and even become bigger in the rock and roll era."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Remarkably Non-Rock and Roll Life
podcast.body: Despite his status as a rock and roll pioneer, Fats Domino led a life that largely deviated from the typical image of rock star excess, save for some drinking and infidelity in the 1950s. He remained married to the same woman for 61 years, rarely traveled beyond his New Orleans home due to a dislike of other foods, and was known for being shy, polite, and genial, avoiding major public scandals. "Other than drinking a bit too much, and sleeping around a little in the 50s, Domino led a remarkably non-rock and roll life."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Unacknowledged Legacy
podcast.body: Despite being, alongside Elvis, the biggest rock and roll star of the 1950s and a profound influence on New Orleans music and artists like Mick Jagger and Leonard Cohen, Fats Domino remains curiously underappreciated in popular consciousness compared to lesser-known figures. This oversight is suggested to stem from racism, either by ignoring him as a black man or because his quiet, polite demeanor did not conform to white prejudices about black artists and their music. "Yet he is curiously unacknowledged in the popular consciousness, while much lesser stars loom larger."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.title: Early Drumming and Diverse Collaborations
xref.body: Chrissy Lee began drumming at age four in a Salvation Army band. Throughout her career, she performed with a wide array of renowned artists including Frank Sinatra, Fats Domino, Tom Jones, and Dinah Washington. She also became heavily involved in education, conducting drum clinics globally. "She started drumming in a Salvation Army band when she was just four years old."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: History of Female Drummers

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
xref.body: Little Richard was an early pioneer of rock and roll, recognized as one of the "piano heroes" who led the genre before the electric guitar became dominant. These pioneers were known for their energetic piano playing, contributing to the "honkin rhythm" that characterized early rock and roll, which evolved from rhythm and blues combos. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Piano Heroes

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
xref.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was a foundational pioneer of rock and roll, counted among the "piano heroes" whose piano playing was central to the genre's initial sound. His style was key in shaping the percussive and energetic rhythm and blues-influenced foundation of early rock. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Piano Heroes

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
xref.body: Ray Charles was an early pioneer of rock and roll, considered one of the "piano heroes" who helped define the genre in its formative years. His piano style was instrumental in blending various musical influences, including jazz and rhythm and blues, into rock and roll. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Piano Heroes

xref.title: Early Rock and Roll Piano Hero
xref.body: Huey Piano Smith was an early pioneer of rock and roll, recognized as one of the "piano heroes" who shaped the genre's sound during its nascent stages. His energetic piano work contributed significantly to the "honkin rhythm" that was a hallmark of early rock and roll. "Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, Fats Domino, Ray Charles, Huey Piano Smith."
